phytosphingosine.summary: A plant- and yeast-derived ceramide building block added to barrier and blemish-prone skincare to ease dryness and help skin look calmer and clearer.

quick.overview:
Phytosphingosine is a fatty-chain amino alcohol that skin cells use to build ceramides, the lipids that hold the skin barrier together. People use it in moisturisers and acne-prone skin products to get less dryness, calmer skin and fewer breakouts.

The chain is simple: it supplies raw material for ceramide synthesis, which supports a stronger barrier, which means less water loss and less irritation. The case for it rests on general ceramide and sphingolipid biology; no human trials of it as a cosmetic were found.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in leave-on moisturisers, serums and blemish-focused products, often alongside ceramides and other barrier lipids. Barrier products are typically used daily, and people usually report changes in dryness over a few weeks.
quick.risks: No cosmetic safety trials were found. The pure chemical carries eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications, which relate to the raw material rather than finished products.

angle.text: Phytosphingosine is a precursor the skin uses to make its own ceramides, so it goes into barrier-repair and blemish-prone skincare to reduce dryness and calm breakouts. A stronger barrier holds more water and irritates less, which reads as smoother, clearer skin.

cholesterol.summary: A barrier lipid that makes up about a quarter of the skin's moisture-holding mortar and is paired with ceramides in repair creams for less dry, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Cholesterol is one of the three main lipids in the outer skin layer, alongside ceramides and free fatty acids. In skincare it is added to barrier-repair moisturisers to help restore dry or damaged skin so it looks smoother and less flaky.

In the skin it packs with ceramides and fatty acids into ordered layers that limit water loss, so adding it supports the moisture barrier. It is used as part of lipid blends; appearance trials of topical cholesterol on its own were not found.
quick.how: People use it through ceramide-based creams and lotions that combine cholesterol, ceramides and fatty acids, applied daily to dry or compromised skin, often after cleansing or bathing. Barrier products are usually judged over a few weeks.
quick.risks: Topical use was not assessed in the sources reviewed. Blood cholesterol is a separate topic: high blood LDL cholesterol is linked to heart disease and handled under clinical guidelines, and that does not concern skincare use.

angle.text: Cholesterol makes up roughly a quarter of the lipid mortar that holds water in the skin, so it is included in ceramide-based moisturisers to restore a dry or damaged barrier. A stronger barrier loses less water, which shows as smoother, less dry skin.

squalene.summary: A skin-identical, lightweight oil used in moisturisers and facial oils to soften skin and add glow without greasiness.

quick.overview:
Squalene is a natural oil the body makes and secretes in skin sebum. In skincare, usually as its stable form squalane, it is used as a light emollient that softens skin and leaves a smoother, glowier finish without a heavy feel.

Because it resembles the skin's own lipids, it blends with the surface oil layer and cuts moisture loss. Toxicology reviews report low toxicity and little allergy at cosmetic levels; no published human trial tested it for acne, ageing or texture.
quick.how: People apply it as a facial oil, or use it as an ingredient in moisturisers, often as a final step to seal in hydration. It is sourced from olive or amaranth oil, shark liver, or made synthetically, and suits many skin types including oily skin.
quick.risks: Reviews report low acute toxicity and little contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations. Squalene has many double bonds, so it can oxidise, which is why the hydrogenated form is common. Shark sourcing has been a conservation concern.

angle.text: Squalene and squalane are light, skin-identical oils that soften skin and add glow without a greasy feel. They sit with the skin's own lipid layer and reduce moisture loss, so skin looks smoother and more supple.

natto-gum.summary: A fermented-soybean water-binding polymer used in face packs and essences to hydrate the surface and leave skin looking plumper and smoother.

quick.overview:
Natto gum is a sticky polymer made by Bacillus fermentation of soybeans, as in the Japanese food natto. It is used in Japanese and Korean face packs, essences and moisturisers to hold water on the skin so the surface looks plumper and smoother.

It is described as a water-binding, film-forming polymer related to poly-gamma-glutamic acid. Its use is documented in patents and product descriptions; no human studies were found.
quick.how: People meet it as an ingredient in sheet masks, wash-off packs, essences and creams, used as a hydration step in layered routines. Hydration effects from this kind of ingredient show up right after application and last while the product is on the skin.
quick.risks: No safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Soy-derived ingredients can be an allergen for some people.

angle.text: Natto gum is a sticky fermented-soybean polymer that holds water on the skin, used in Japanese and Korean face packs and essences. A better-hydrated surface looks plumper and smoother; its use is documented in patents and product descriptions.

lauric-acid.summary: A coconut-derived fatty acid that cleanses as a soap raw material and is applied by some users to reduce acne bacteria for clearer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Lauric acid is the main fatty acid in coconut oil and a raw material for soaps and cleansers. Some people apply it with the aim of cutting back acne-causing bacteria so skin looks clearer.

The idea comes from lab work: a 1972 study of 30 fatty acids found it the most inhibitory saturated fatty acid against Gram-positive bacteria, and it disrupts bacterial membranes in lab tests. Trials on skin for acne or appearance were not found.
quick.how: Most people meet it as a cleansing agent in soaps and face washes, or through coconut-oil products. It is used as a rinse-off or leave-on ingredient and sometimes combined with other acne products.
quick.risks: Pure lauric acid can irritate skin and eyes. Eating it raises total and LDL cholesterol in trials, which matters for people managing cardiovascular risk.

angle.text: Lauric acid, abundant in coconut oil, is used in cleansers and applied by some people to reduce acne bacteria for clearer skin. Lab studies show it inhibits certain bacteria; skin trials for acne were not found.

panthenol.summary: Provitamin B5 humectant in moisturisers, hair products and wound creams that hydrates skin, calms irritation and leaves skin and hair smoother.

quick.overview:
Panthenol is a vitamin B5 derivative found in moisturisers, shampoos, lip care and healing ointments. It is used to hydrate skin, calm irritation and leave skin and hair feeling softer and smoother.

Skin converts it to pantothenic acid, which is used to make coenzyme A, and it binds water as a humectant. Studies and reviews describe hydration and post-procedure wound-healing roles for dexpanthenol; hair-growth claims lack trial support in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is applied in leave-on moisturisers and serums, as an ingredient in conditioners and shampoos, and in ointments such as Bepanthen for dry, irritated or healing skin. It is a routine ingredient in barrier and post-procedure care.
quick.risks: It is generally well tolerated; rare contact dermatitis or allergy has been reported.

angle.text: Panthenol converts to vitamin B5 in the skin and draws water in as a humectant, so it goes into moisturisers, hair products and wound creams. Skin looks softer and calmer, and human data mainly cover hydration and wound healing.

jojoba-oil.summary: A sebum-like liquid wax used as a facial moisturiser and carrier oil to soften skin and hair.

quick.overview:
Jojoba oil is a golden liquid wax from a desert shrub, widely used as a facial moisturiser, carrier oil and hair treatment. People use it to soften dry skin and hair and get a smoother look.

About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters that resemble the skin's own sebum, and it forms a stable layer on skin that reduces water loss, according to oil-comparison studies. Controlled trials on appearance are limited.
quick.how: It is used as a few drops on the face or hair, as a carrier for other oils, or as an ingredient in moisturisers and conditioners. Many people with oily or combination skin choose it for its light feel. It is a daily-use product judged by how skin feels over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Rare contact dermatitis has been reported. It is a cosmetic oil, not intended for eating.

angle.text: Jojoba oil is a liquid wax whose esters resemble skin's own sebum, so it is used as a facial moisturiser and carrier oil. It forms a stable layer that cuts moisture loss, leaving skin and hair softer and smoother.

tamanu-oil.summary: A Pacific nut oil used to help fade scars and acne marks and calm breakouts, drawing on traditional use for wounds and burns.

quick.overview:
Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil from the nuts of a coastal tropical tree, used in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for wounds, burns and skin conditions. In natural skincare it is used to fade scars and acne marks and calm breakouts.

In cell studies a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion raised skin-cell proliferation and collagen production, and the oil shows antioxidant activity. Human trials for scars or acne were not found.
quick.how: People apply it as a few drops directly on marks or scars, or mix it into creams and carrier oils, usually over weeks to months. Its strong scent and thick texture mean it is often blended.
quick.risks: It is reported as low in toxicity at low concentrations; allergy data are limited. As a nut-derived oil it may matter to people with nut allergy.

angle.text: Tamanu oil is used to fade scars and acne marks and calm breakouts, building on traditional Pacific use for wounds and burns. Lab studies on skin cells show raised proliferation and collagen production; human trials were not found.

meadowfoam-seed-oil.summary: A very stable plant oil from a Californian and Oregon wildflower, used in creams, lip products and hair care to soften skin and add shine.

quick.overview:
Meadowfoam seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Limnanthes alba, a wildflower native to California and Oregon. It is used in creams, lip products and hair care as a light emollient that softens skin and adds shine.

Its fatty acids are mostly very long-chain types, which the sources link to its unusual resistance to going rancid. A 2021 cosmetic-science study tested it as a pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick; human skin-benefit trials were not found.
quick.how: People meet it as an ingredient in moisturisers, lipsticks and balms, hair serums and conditioners, or as a carrier oil. Its stability is a main reason formulators choose it, so it appears in long-shelf-life products.
quick.risks: Unpurified meadowfoam oil is not suitable for eating because of its high erucic acid. Topical safety data from clinical studies were not found. The plant's commercial crops have been vulnerable to fungal disease.

angle.text: Meadowfoam seed oil is a light, very oxidation-stable emollient used in creams, lip products and hair care. It softens skin and adds shine, and its stability is the main reason formulators use it.

sea-buckthorn-oil.summary: A carotenoid-rich orange oil from Hippophae berries and seeds, used in creams and supplements to moisturise and support skin repair and glow.

quick.overview:
Sea buckthorn oil is taken from the berry pulp and seeds of a hardy shrub of Europe and Asia. The pulp oil is orange to deep red, rich in carotenoids and palmitoleic acid. It goes into creams, lotions and supplements promoted for moisturising, glow and skin repair.

Proponents credit carotenoids, vitamin E, sterols and unsaturated fatty acids for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Lab work on human skin cells found seed oil altered lipid changes induced by UV exposure. Published human trials cover dry eye and other mucosal conditions; a skin-aging trial was registered in 2008 but published skin results were not found.
quick.how: People use it as an ingredient in creams and serums, as a few drops of oil on skin, or as an oral supplement. Pulp oil can tint skin and fabric orange. Results are generally assessed over weeks.
quick.risks: Reviews describe the oil as generally well tolerated in the trials cited, but safety data specific to cosmetic use are limited. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and food supplement; regulatory status varies by country.

angle.text: Sea buckthorn oil supplies carotenoids and unsaturated fatty acids with antioxidant activity, and is used in creams and supplements for moisturising, glow and skin repair. Human trials have mostly covered dry eye and mucosal dryness.

evening-primrose-oil.summary: A gamma-linolenic acid-rich seed oil taken as a supplement or applied to dry, eczema-prone or breakout-prone skin to help it look calmer and less dry.

quick.overview:
Evening primrose oil is pressed from the seeds of Oenothera biennis, a North American plant, and is rich in linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA). People take it as a supplement or apply it to dry, eczema-prone or hormonally breakout-prone skin to get calmer, less dry-looking skin.

GLA is an omega-6 fatty acid the body converts to prostaglandin precursors, and proponents argue this supports skin barrier and inflammatory balance. It has been studied for atopic eczema, breast pain and menopausal symptoms; a Cochrane review found no effect on eczema, and the US NCCIH describes the evidence as insufficient for any medical condition.
quick.how: It is mostly taken as capsules, with some people applying the oil or using skincare products containing it. People commonly use it daily for several weeks or months and pair it with a moisturiser routine.
quick.risks: Described as likely safe at recommended amounts, with headache and nausea reported. It may raise bleeding risk, and sources advise caution in people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

angle.text: Evening primrose oil supplies gamma-linolenic acid, which proponents say supports the skin barrier and calms inflammation, so it is taken or applied for dry, eczema-prone or breakout-prone skin. Reviews of its use for eczema find insufficient evidence.

macadamia-oil.summary: A palmitoleic- and oleic-rich nut oil used as a rich emollient in moisturisers, body oils and hair products for a softer, more supple look.

quick.overview:
Macadamia oil is pressed from the kernels of Macadamia integrifolia, native to eastern Australia. It is mostly monounsaturated, with oleic acid and an unusual amount of palmitoleic acid, a fatty acid also found in skin sebum. It is used in moisturisers, body oils and hair products for a softer, more supple look.

In products it works as an emollient and fragrance fixative, and its low polyunsaturated content is linked to good oxidative stability. Research covers its fatty acids and stability and dietary palmitoleic acid and blood lipids; trials on skin appearance were not found.
quick.how: People use it as a body or facial oil, as a hair oil, or as an ingredient in creams and lip products. It is also a cooking oil, and it is generally a daily moisturising step.
quick.risks: Specific topical safety data were not described in the sources. As a tree-nut product it can matter to people with nut allergy.

angle.text: Macadamia oil is a rich emollient used in moisturisers, body oils and hair products, with interest in its palmitoleic acid, which is also found in skin sebum. It softens skin and hair so they look smoother and more supple.

grapeseed-oil.summary: A light, linoleic-rich winemaking by-product used as a facial and massage oil for moisture without heaviness.

quick.overview:
Grapeseed oil is pressed from seeds left over from winemaking. It is mostly linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid found in skin lipids, with a light texture. People use it as a facial, body and massage oil, especially those with oily or breakout-prone skin who want moisture without greasiness.

Linoleic-rich oils are a common emollient choice. The sources do not report mechanistic studies of grapeseed oil on skin, and trials on skin appearance were not found.
quick.how: It is applied as a few drops on the face or body, used for massage, blended into hair care, or included in cosmetics. It is also a cooking oil. It is typically used as a daily lightweight moisturising oil.
quick.risks: Some batches have been found to contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from combustion gases during seed drying. Its high polyunsaturated content makes it prone to oxidation.

angle.text: Grapeseed oil is a lightweight, linoleic-rich oil used for facial and massage use by people who want moisture without heaviness, often those with oily or breakout-prone skin. It leaves skin softer and less dry-looking.

black-rice-extract.summary: An anthocyanin-rich antioxidant extract from pigmented rice, promoted in anti-aging and brightening skincare to limit visible signs of skin aging.

quick.overview:
Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation from the bran of dark-coloured rice, concentrated in anthocyanins. It is marketed in supplements and skincare as an antioxidant botanical, promoted for anti-aging and a brighter look.

The idea is that anthocyanin antioxidants reduce oxidative stress on skin, so fewer signs of aging show. Lab studies report it raised antioxidant enzyme activity in cells and mice and reduced inflammatory signalling in macrophage cells. Small human trials are registered on metabolic, cognitive and immune outcomes; ones on skin appearance were not found.
quick.how: People use it in serums and creams, or as a supplement, usually as part of a broader antioxidant or brightening routine. Results are judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No safety signals are described in the sources, and rice-based foods are widely eaten. Extract-specific safety data from human trials were not found. Anthocyanin stability and bioavailability are active research topics.

angle.text: Black rice extract is promoted in anti-aging and brightening skincare for its anthocyanin pigments, which act as antioxidants to ease oxidative stress on skin. Lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity; human skin trials were not found.

propolis.summary: Bee-resin K-beauty extract used in ampoules and creams to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish.

quick.overview:
Propolis is the resin bees blend with wax to seal their hives. A K-beauty staple in ampoules and creams, it is used to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish, building on a long folk-medicine history.

Lab studies attribute antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity to its flavonoids and phenolics, including CAPE, which inhibits NF-kappa B signalling in cell experiments. Composition varies widely by origin. Human trials on cosmetic skin outcomes were not found; registered clinical trials concern uses such as oral health.
quick.how: People use propolis ampoules, creams and spot treatments as part of layered K-beauty routines, often for blemish-prone, irritated or dull skin. It is also sold as a supplement.
quick.risks: Contact allergy is the main documented risk, with skin inflammation and lip swelling reported from topical products, especially in people sensitive to bee products. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and supplement; no special approval for skin benefits is reported.

angle.text: Propolis is used in K-beauty ampoules and creams to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish. Lab studies show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity; skin-specific human trials were not found.

honey-topical.summary: A moisture-drawing pantry staple used in masks for soft, hydrated, brighter-looking skin, with wound-care research behind its use on skin.

quick.overview:
Topical honey is used as a mask or skincare ingredient for hydration and a softer, brighter look. It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water at the skin surface, and it has a long folk history on burns and wounds.

Its antibacterial properties are attributed to compounds such as methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, under preliminary study. Trials exist for wounds, mouth ulcers and eye conditions, and medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns; trials on cosmetic brightening were not found.
quick.how: People apply it as a thin layer for a short wash-off mask, mix it with ingredients such as oats or yoghurt, or use it as an ingredient in cleansers and creams. Hydration shows right after rinsing.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated as a food. Infant botulism is the best-documented risk of honey, so it is not given to infants under one, and allergy is possible in sensitive people.

angle.text: Honey draws moisture into the skin surface, so it is used in masks and skincare for softer, hydrated, glowier-looking skin, and some people use it for brightening and blemishes. Its documented research is in wound care.

bee-venom-topical.summary: Korean 'faux-tox' bee-venom cream marketed as a natural alternative to botulinum toxin to tighten skin and soften expression lines.

quick.overview:
Bee venom creams and masks are marketed in Korean skincare as a gentler stand-in for botulinum toxin injections. Brands say they tighten the skin and smooth expression lines.

Honey bee venom is a mix of peptides and enzymes; melittin is about half of the peptides, and the creams are thought to work by a mild tingling or plumping effect on the surface. The sources do not show how a cream would deliver them through skin to relax facial muscle. Wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found; the one controlled human study identified tested an ointment on jaw-muscle tension.
quick.how: People apply it as a cream, serum or mask in an evening routine, often around the forehead and eyes, and generally judge results over weeks. It is positioned as a non-injection option.
quick.risks: Phospholipase A2 in the venom is a main allergen, and venom can cause local inflammation. Bee-sting allergy is a reason to avoid it. Data on cosmetic-product safety were not found.

angle.text: Topical bee venom is marketed in Korean skincare as a natural 'faux-tox' that tightens skin and smooths expression lines. The venom's peptides are bioactive in the lab, but wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found.

galactomyces-ferment-filtrate.summary: Sake-yeast ferment behind Japanese and Korean essences such as Pitera, used for brightening, hydration and a smoother glow.

quick.overview:
Galactomyces ferment filtrate (GFF) is made by fermenting with Galactomyces yeast and is the base of essences such as Pitera. People use it for hydration, a smoother texture and a brighter, more even glow. Its origin story traces to sake brewers whose hands stayed youthful-looking.

Cell studies report changes in keratinocyte differentiation, barrier-related proteins and inflammatory signalling, though the active compounds are unidentified. Product studies, including a multi-year longitudinal study, report improvements in pores, roughness and pigmentation, but they test formulas with other ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to GFF alone.
quick.how: It is used as an essence or toner-style step after cleansing, patted on before serums and moisturiser, and sits in many daily Japanese and Korean routines. Users generally report changes over weeks.
quick.risks: Patch tests are reported as non-irritating in secondary sources. No serious safety signals were found in the sources reviewed, though long-term data are limited.

angle.text: Galactomyces ferment filtrate, sold in essences such as Pitera, delivers a yeast ferment of vitamins and amino acids for hydration, brighter tone and a smoother glow. Cell-lab and product studies report improved pores, roughness and pigmentation, though those products had other ingredients too.

bifida-ferment-lysate.summary: Probiotic-derived ferment in repair and barrier serums, used to soothe skin, build resilience and support a more youthful look.

quick.overview:
Bifida ferment lysate (BFL) is made by fermenting Bifidobacterium and breaking down the cells. It is added to repair and barrier serums as a probiotic-derived, or postbiotic, active promoted for soothing, resilience and a more youthful look.

The chain is a stronger barrier and less stress damage, so skin looks calmer and healthier. A 2023 cell study reported strengthened barrier function and stable skin defence signalling; human studies tested multi-ingredient products, so BFL's own effect is unclear. Bifidobacterium itself has been studied for acne and atopic dermatitis.
quick.how: People use it in serums, creams and ampoules for barrier repair, typically in daily morning or evening routines, often with other soothing ingredients. Barrier benefits are generally judged over weeks.
quick.risks: No specific harms were found in the reviewed sources. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug.

angle.text: Bifida ferment lysate is a probiotic-derived ingredient used in repair and barrier serums to soothe skin and build resilience. A stronger barrier and less stress damage show as calmer, healthier-looking skin; lab barrier data exist and human trials have used combination products.

lactobacillus-ferment.summary: Probiotic ferment in K-beauty creams used for barrier support and for calming sensitive or reddened skin.

quick.overview:
Lactobacillus ferment is made by fermenting with Lactobacillus bacteria and appears in K-beauty and probiotic skincare creams. People use it for barrier support and to calm sensitive or reddened skin so it looks less reactive.

Postbiotic ingredients are proposed to influence the skin microbiome and barrier signalling, though mechanisms for this specific ferment were not shown. The closest human study found was a scalp-microbiome study of a combined Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in daily creams, serums and toners aimed at sensitive or reactive skin, often alongside other barrier and soothing ingredients. Results are typically judged over a few weeks.
quick.risks: No specific harms were documented in the sources reviewed. Postbiotics are not a separate regulatory category and are assessed under existing frameworks case by case.

angle.text: Lactobacillus ferment is a probiotic-derived ingredient in K-beauty creams, used to support the barrier and calm sensitive or reddened skin. Skin looks less reactive as the barrier steadies, though skin-specific human evidence is limited.
